sentences.text: Mohamed Salah, and the ghosts of Egypt's golden generation.
By Patricia Sabga, for Al Jazeera.
Salah has previously taken flak from Egypt's fans.
Now he leads an undefeated team into the round of 16 against Argentina, and a nation is daring to believe again.
For some Egyptian football fans, watching Mohamed Salah qualify with Egypt for two World Cups will never make up for the fact that the golden generation did not get their shot in 2006, 2010, or 2014.
It is unfair to compare the two generations, says Ahmed Elshiekh, a former national team player.
The golden generation did everything but get to the World Cup.
They beat Italy when they were world champions.
The draw was just unkind to them.
Salah is the captain and leader of the current generation.
He won every trophy on offer during a glittering nine-year career at Liverpool, that made him the highest-scoring foreigner in Premier League history.
Given his status, it is perhaps no surprise that he shouldered the blame for a continental drought stretching back to 2010.
The failures compounded.
The 2021 final, lost to Senegal on penalties.
Then a World Cup playoff against the same opponent, lost the same way.
In the first shootout, Salah, listed fifth, never got his kick.
In the second, he went first, and missed.
To soothe the pain, fans clung to the team crowned African champions in 2006, 2008, and 2010, led by Mohamed Aboutrika.
But this time feels different.
Egypt qualified for 2026 undefeated, winning eight of ten.
A second-half comeback against New Zealand delivered the nation's first-ever World Cup win.
Salah left the Iran game with a hamstring injury, then played all 120 minutes of the shootout win over Australia, converting his kick with a Panenka.
This Egypt team is better than any we have seen in years, yet is still remarkably fragile.
On Saturday, against Argentina, a golden generation's ghosts will either be laid to rest, or rise once more.
